LINE PROJECT IN BELL, BURNET,                      §
CONCHO, CORYELL, LAMPASAS,                         §

MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, SAN SABA,                    §
SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN, AND                         §
WILLIAMSON COUNTIES                                §



              INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF OF MEYER E11 INTERVENORS

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

           COMES NOW Paul & Jane Meyer Family Foundation, SM Retreat Ltd. and Leslie Meyer

Rhea [“Meyer E11 Intervenors”], and pursuant to SOAH Orders No. 6 and 32 file this Initial Post-

Hearing Brief of Meyer E11 Intervenors in the above-entitled docket:

      I.          Statement of Position

           The Meyer E11 Intervenors are not advocating for any particular route. The Meyer E11

Intervenors, as would be expected, are opposed to any route that includes links E6, E7, E8, E11

and E12. In short, we are opposed to any route that cuts through the City of Belton and the north

side of Salado, i.e. the northern routes in the eastern half of the study area.

     II.          Community Values

           One of the most important criteria, which arguably is also a component of each of the other

PURA criteria, is community values. What does the local community in the study area hold

important?

                                                                                                Page 1
        As reflected in the Environmental Assessment, the community members that attended the

open house events expressed significant concerns regarding routing close to habitable structures

and fragmentation of private property by not paralleling property lines. Joint Applicants’ Exhibit

1, pp. 203-204. There were also specific community comments that routing should “minimize

removal of existing oak trees” and protect Texas historical sites including “sites and landmarks

dating back to the 1800s that hold significant cultural and community importance.” Joint

Applicants’ Exhibit 1, pp. 204 and 206. Before embarking on a route-level analysis, it is worth

examining some of the expressed community values at a link level.

       Ordinarily a link-level review of habitable structures would not be productive, but in this

study area the numbers are so dramatic they deserve mention. As was well-illustrated by Hodge-

Schwertner Exhibit 12, despite being relatively short in length Links E6 and E12 have more

habitable structures than any other link by far. This fact led witnesses like the Joint Applicants’

panel, Rae Lynn Schneider Reinecke and PUC Staff witness John Poole to independently

recommend against inclusion of Links E6 and E 12 in any selected route. Cherokee Creek Exhibit

1, pp. 24-25 and Staff Exhibit 1, pp. 38-39; RR v.2, 54:6-55:17; RR v.3, 267:6-268:11. As noted

in the testimony and by reference to the maps in the case, any route that would include Link E11

by necessity includes either E6 or E12.

       The community values comment about not removing existing oak trees is particularly

significant when examining Link E11. The record reflects that there are several centuries-old oak

trees on Link E11. CBF Ranch Exhibit 1, pp. 3-4. As expressed in the testimony of PUC Staff

witness John Poole, the removal of trees of such age and stature not only raise environmental

concerns, but also cultural, historical and community values. RR v.2, 270:1-271:13. Such




                                                                                             Page 2
 landmark trees require independent consideration beyond mere statistics regarding length of

woodland crossing.

           Finally, the historic Summers Mill structure on the Meyer E11 properties certainly qualifies

as the expressed community value of preserving Texas historical structures. It was built in 1866,

served as a post office for the community, and has been a registered Texas Historical Site since

1965. Meyer E11 Exhibit 1, pp. 7, 11 and 14. Routing 200-foot tall towers and 200-foot wide

clear-cut right-of-way near a structure that has been preserved for over 160 years in its natural and

historical context would be a total disregard for the expressed community value of preserving

Texas and local history.

           Perhaps an even stronger expression of community values unfolded during these very

proceedings. It is very significant that not one of the Routes of Interest generated by the

intervenors in these proceedings included Links E6, E7, E8, E11 or E12.. Joint App. Ex. 22 and

23. Of all the intervenors, only one group advocated during the hearing for Route 392. As will be

discussed below, there is no evidentiary support for this selection.

    III.          Route-Level Analysis

        While there are some variations, the primary routes discussed during the hearing were the

Joint Applicants’ recommendation of Route 894 and PUC Staff’s recommendation of Route 487.

The Brady Creek Intervenors advocated for Route 392 during the hearing, but drew little support

while generating significant opposition. A route-level analysis of the end-to-end data – as is

required in this process – reveals the evidentiary basis for the opposition. Not only are Routes 894

and 487 superior in a holistic analysis, but Route 392 is a statistical outlier that is not remotely

comparable.




                                                                                                 Page 3
        As was pointed out repeatedly in the testimony and is reflected in the Joint Applicants’

data, the so-called “Northern corridor” route is both longer and more expensive than the

recommended Routes 894 and 487. In fact, it is one of the few Routes of Interest that costs over

$1.7 billion dollars. Joint Applicants’ Exhibit 23.

       It is in other routing factors that the differences are much larger and reveal what an outlier

the minority route truly is. The most-discussed factor during the hearing was habitable structures,

and the contrast could not be more clear. Fully acknowledging that there were habitable structures

not included in the Joint Applicants’ data – including the house on CBF Ranch on Link E11 (CBF

Ranch Exhibit 1) – using the Joint Applicants’ data for simplicity shows that the minority route

impacts 60% more habitable structures than Route 894 and almost 42% more than Route 487.

Such differences are not just significant, they are breathtaking. Adding more than half-again as

many habitable structures to a route is the exact opposite of prudent avoidance.

       While habitable structures, cost and length are traditionally important factors in PUC

routing determinations, they are not the only three factors that support a selection of either of the

recommended routes. The following is a list of routing factors in which minority Route 392 is

inferior to both Routes 894 and 487 and the extent of the difference between the best of the three

and 392:

     1)        Total length paralleling compatible ROW (19.5% less)
     2)        Crossing potential wetlands (22.8% more)
     3)        Stream crossings (14.9% more)
     4)        Recorded cultural resource sites crossed (8 times as many)
     5)        Cultural resource sites w/in 1,000 feet (almost 3 times as many)
     6)        Length over high archeological/historical potential (28.4% more)
     7)        FAA-registered airports (50% more)
     8)        FM/microwave installations (more than twice as many)
     9)        Highway crossings (16 2/3% more)
    10)        FM/County road crossings (55.3% more)
    11)        Foreground visual zone of highways (88% more)



                                                                                               Page 4
 The “Northern Corridor” route is also the only one of the three that crosses any upland woodland

areas, parallels streams, or is near heliports and AM transmitters. Joint Applicants’ Exhibit 23

(Route by Miles tab).

       By any form of holistic review of the routing factors in PURA and the PUC rules, Brady

Creek’s advocacy of Route 392 is completely unsupported by the evidence in the record. It is not

only significantly inferior on the factors that the Commissioners tend to find significant, it is

significantly worse – sometimes by orders of magnitude – on most of the routing factors in the

Joint Applicants’ data table. Perhaps of greater importance, the minority route also ignores many

of the community values expressed during the open houses.              The community comments

specifically called out residences, property fragmentation, trees and historical sites. Route 392

impacts 60% more habitable structures, parallels 30.9% less apparent property boundaries, is the

only route of the three that crosses woodlands (including the centuries old trees on Link E11), and

has enormously greater impact on cultural resources and archeological sites. Through their

comments at the open houses the community expressed that they do not value the “Northern

Corridor” route.

    IV.          Conclusion

          The required holistic review of the routing factors set forth in PURA and the PUC rules

would support either the Joint Applicants’ selection of Route 894 or PUC Staff’s recommendation

of Route 487. Either choice would also have many supporters among the intervenors in this case.

By contrast, there is virtually no intervenor support for Route 392 because the record is irrefutably

against it. It is not an inferior route or even a poor route. In an end-to-end route-level analysis,

any selection of Route 392 would be utterly irresponsible and an abrogation of the routing factors

in PURA and the PUC rules. The Meyer E11 Intervenors ask that after due consideration of the



                                                                                               Page 5
 evidentiary record and all the routing factors the judges select a route that does not include Links

E6, E7, E8, E11 and E12.
